slides: Welcome back. Products of numbers in a row, and of even numbers, follow some very handy rules. Let's build them.

slides.say: Remember, two numbers in a row always divide by two, and three in a row by six.

Four in a row. One of them divides by four, and another one is even, so that's eight. And one of them divides by three. Eight and three share nothing, so the product divides by eight times three, twenty-four.
Let's see it in numbers. One times two times three times four is twenty-four. Two times three times four times five is a hundred twenty, five twenty-fours.
at: Two times three times four times

slides.say: Now even numbers. Each even number is two times something, so two evens together are four times something. Two times six is twelve, and four times ten is forty, both divide by four.
at: Each even number is two times

slides.say: Two consecutive even numbers are even better. One of them always divides by four, and the other by two, so the product divides by eight. Two times four is eight, six times eight is forty-eight, and ten times twelve is a hundred twenty, fifteen eights.

Is a fraction a whole number? Count the twos. m is even and n is odd. m squared over eight, times n plus one. m is even, so m squared has at least two twos. n is odd, so n plus one is even, one more two. Three twos on top, and eight is two times two times two. It cancels, always whole.
Let's check. m is two and n is one, four times two over eight is one. m is two and n is three, four times four over eight is two.
at: m is two and n is one
m is two and n is three

slides.say: But m times n plus one, over eight, has only two twos for sure. With m two and n one, two times two over eight is a half. Not whole.

On the exam, the products hide inside expressions. x squared minus one is x minus one, times x plus one, the neighbors of x.
